questions.stem: A car of mass 1200 kg is travelling at 10 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?
questions.explanation: KE = 1/2 x m x v^2 = 1/2 x 1200 x 10^2 = 1/2 x 1200 x 100 = 60 000 J. A common mistake is forgetting to square the velocity (which would give 6 000 J) or forgetting the 1/2 (which would give 120 000 J).

questions.stem: If the speed of an object doubles, what happens to its kinetic energy?
questions.explanation: KE = 1/2 x m x v^2. Since velocity is squared in the formula, doubling the speed means KE increases by 2^2 = 4 times. This is why speed is so important for road safety: doubling your speed quadruples the kinetic energy that must be dissipated in a crash.

questions.stem: A cyclist and bicycle have a combined mass of 80 kg and kinetic energy of 1 000 J. What is their speed?
questions.explanation: Rearranging KE = 1/2 x m x v^2 gives v^2 = 2 x KE / m = 2 x 1000 / 80 = 25. So v = sqrt(25) = 5 m/s. Option A (25 m/s) is the result if you forget to take the square root. Option C (12.5) results from dividing KE by mass without the factor of 2.

questions.stem: Two balls are thrown: Ball X has mass 0.5 kg at 8 m/s, and Ball Y has mass 2 kg at 4 m/s. Which has more kinetic energy?

options.text: Ball X, because it is faster
Ball Y, because it is heavier
They have the same kinetic energy
Cannot determine without knowing the height

questions.explanation: Ball X: KE = 1/2 x 0.5 x 8^2 = 1/2 x 0.5 x 64 = 16 J. Ball Y: KE = 1/2 x 2 x 4^2 = 1/2 x 2 x 16 = 16 J. Both have 16 J. Speed is more important than mass because it is squared, but in this case the values balance out. Height is irrelevant for kinetic energy.

questions.stem: A 0.1 kg tennis ball is hit and gains 20 J of kinetic energy. What is the approximate speed of the ball?
questions.explanation: v^2 = 2 x KE / m = 2 x 20 / 0.1 = 400. So v = sqrt(400) = 20 m/s. Option A (200 m/s) results from forgetting to square root. Option C (400) is v^2, not v. Option D would result from an incorrect rearrangement.
